summary: A note from Bob Braden at UCLA's Campus Computing Network about the ASCII and EBCDIC mapping used by NETRJS, its remote job entry service. Users of ASCII hosts had found problems with the original mapping rules, so CCN changed the mapping and added a new one. The RFC tells users, alerts the RJE protocol committee, and acknowledges Joel Winett's earlier work.

plainLanguage.summary: NETRJS translates characters between network users and an EBCDIC mainframe. This note revises the translation rules and adds a mapping for a Teletype terminal.

subtitle: Updated character mappings for NETRJS users with ASCII, EBCDIC, and Teletype terminals.

tldr.problem: NETRJS connects ASCII users to an IBM system that processes data in EBCDIC, and users found problems in the earlier character mappings.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC revises mappings for ASCII graphics that EBCDIC lacks and adds a TTY terminal type for Model 33/35 Teletypes.
tldr.outcome: The author concludes that a server may need several translation tables for different terminal character sets.

today: The unit metadata lists RFC 338 as Unknown, with no RFC recorded as updating or obsoleting it. The text documents character mapping for one early remote job service.

sections.title: Translation for Network RJE
sections.content:
NETRJS lets a remote user submit batch work to UCLA's IBM 360/91. When the virtual terminal uses ASCII, CCN translates the incoming card-reader stream to EBCDIC and translates printer output back to ASCII.

Users at several ASCII hosts reported weaknesses in the original mapping, so CCN changed the mapping and added another terminal type.
sections.plainLanguage: The mainframe and many network hosts use different character codes. NETRJS translates input and output so they can exchange text.

sections.title: ASCII and EBCDIC Mappings
sections.content:
The RFC describes the basic EBCDIC graphics and explains that six ASCII graphics have no matching character in EBCDIC: square brackets, braces, caret, and backtick. The earlier NETRJS mapping turned these characters into question marks.

The revised table maps those six graphics to specified EBCDIC codes, so a user can transmit ASCII text that includes them.
sections.plainLanguage: Some characters exist in ASCII but not in the EBCDIC set used by the mainframe. The new mapping gives those characters distinct codes instead of replacing them with question marks.

sections.title: A Mapping for Teletype Users
sections.content:
The RFC adds TTY as a virtual remote batch terminal type alongside ASCII and EBCDIC. A user can select it by connecting to the specified socket or by entering the TTYRJS command after connecting through socket 1.

The TTY mapping accounts for characters such as the up-arrow and left-arrow graphics on Model 33/35 Teletypes. The author concludes that one pair of translation tables cannot serve every terminal type.
sections.plainLanguage: Model 33/35 Teletypes use some keys that differ from ASCII. NETRJS adds a separate mode to translate those keys for the mainframe.
